transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-04-05 17:30 PDT
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Rao (Redwood SE), Ethan Cho (Redwood CSM); Marcus Lee (Aegis Head of Platform), Sara Patel (NetEng), Daniel Ortiz (CTO), Leah Wong (SRE)

Summary:
Quick heatcheck on VPC routing stability after last kernel upgrade; review of recent p99 spikes, discussion of sticky routing/session affinity, fallbacks and circuit-breaker thresholds; agreement on targeted bench runs and artifact handoff (pcap/traces), plus a short runbook for emergency rollback.

Topics: routing jitter, MTU mismatches, KV cache warmup, prefix caching, canary rollout sizing, SSO/KMS audit artifacts, SOC2 ask, next pilot steps.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan Kim: hey everyone thanks for joining uh we've got about 45 minutes, quick heatcheck on the VPC routing issues post-kernel patch. Priya and I will run through logs then hand to Marcus and team for what you saw.
[00:18] Marcus Lee: thanks jordan, yeah uh we saw three p99 spikes yesterday after the deploy at 02:10 UTC. spikes aligned with a wide rollout to the east region. important note: latency went from ~130ms p99 to around 420ms for short periods. not constant but, um, large enough to trigger our circuit breakers.
[00:42] Priya Rao: do you still have the traceroutes and pcap from those windows? that would help us see if this is intra-datacenter routing or an egress path.
[00:51] Sara Patel: yes i've uploaded a set to the shared folder, there's also a couple of packet captures, i'll link later. some of the traces show path change mid-session, like BGP flapping or our ORT doing a reroute.
[01:08] Jordan Kim: okay interesting. from our side the kernel upgrade introduced a new batching kernel and also a small change in our session affinity hashing to improve KV cache locality, but that could have caused sticky sessions to move unexpectedly. we called it out in the release notes but maybe not clear enough.
[01:29] Leah Wong: yeah we noticed session affinity felt less sticky, we had more cache misses which spiked our token cost and latency. is that expected from the change?
[01:38] Priya Rao: the intent was to improve long-running sessions by grouping similar sequence-length requests for better batch packing, so normally you'd see fewer cache misses. however if routing reassignments happen mid-kv-warmup you can get double misses. that might explain the spike.
[01:58] Daniel Ortiz: is there a fallback to the older hashing if we detect cache thrash? like an automatic fallback? we can't have production user flows hit 400ms p99 intermittently.
[02:12] Priya Rao: we do have a circuit-breaker policy in the runtime — it's pluggable. currently it's tuned to fail-over to a compat model variant, but not to revert hashing. we can add a quick override that pins to legacy hashing on failure, that's a small config change.
[02:31] Marcus Lee: that would be ideal. we also had a related problem where egress MTU mismatches amplified retransmits during the spike. anyone else seen MTU issues post-upgrade?
[02:44] Jordan Kim: we saw a couple reports in staging where jumbo frames were mis-negotiated after the NIC firmware bump. firmware + kernel combos can do weird things with offload. Ethan, notes?
[02:55] Ethan Cho: yeah there was a micro-change in the kernel netstack path we enabled for perf; it toggles GRO/GSO defaults. usually good for throughput but can expose a mismatch if the path assumes certain MTU.
[03:12] Sara Patel: hmm that matches what we saw—lossy retransmits and bursts that pushed the ingress queue. we also saw gRPC keepalive flaps during the window.
[03:25] Priya Rao: ok for immediate mitigation we recommend 1) rolling back the netstack toggle in the canary group, 2) enabling legacy session hashing in the runtime for that canary, and 3) run a packet-level bench with prefix caching on/off to quantify the delta.
[03:45] Marcus Lee: timeline? can you push a canary rollback today?
[03:48] Jordan Kim: we could push a targeted rollback to the two affected AZs today, yes, assuming you sign off. it's a low-risk change to the kernel flags, not the full model artifact.
[03:59] Leah Wong: we'll need the rollback runbook and an SLA window. also want to see the audit trail—who triggered what—so we can map to our change advisory.
[04:09] Jordan Kim: understood, we'll produce an abbreviated rollback runbook and a short changelog. Priya will include the config toggles and an example grpc/keepalive tuning snippet.
[04:19] Daniel Ortiz: on the security side, can you confirm whether the logs include KMS access events for the cache encryption? and do you have the SOC2 artifact we requested?
[04:30] Ethan Cho: yes the runtime writes key access events to the audit log, we can provide a filtered export. the SOC2 packet is in our security docs repo; I'll attach the attestation and the latest PCA.
[04:42] Marcus Lee: great, we need that to clear our legal/security gate. also our procurement asked about Dedicated capacity pricing if we need guaranteed throughput during cutover.
[04:53] Jordan Kim: we'll pull a Dedicated SKU quote, but as a pilot we recommend targeted canaries first. Dedicated is an option if you want reserved GPU pools; pricing varies by commit. I'll have sales follow up.
[05:06] Sara Patel: quick technical q — when you say prefix cache, are you referring to the prefix-based KV cache that Redwood described, or client-side prefix heuristics? we saw different results depending on whether prefix caching was warm.
[05:20] Priya Rao: prefix-based KV cache in the runtime; it stores partial KV segments so warm prefixes reduce per-token compute. client-side heuristics help request shaping but don't replace the runtime cache. in our bench we want to control for client-side shaping.
[05:37] Marcus Lee: we've been running with a short TTL on prefix cache to be conservative, maybe that's hurting us. what's recommended TTL for typical healthcare latency-sensitive workloads?
[05:46] Priya Rao: for chatty workloads we recommend a 10-30s TTL and a small cache size per shard; for long sequential inference, longer TTLs work better. given your burst patterns I'd start with 15s and measure.
[05:59] Leah Wong: ok we'll try 15s. also can you send a small script to replay the failing windows with preserved timing so we can run locally?
[06:08] Jordan Kim: yes Priya will put together a reproducible bench script with preserved inter-arrival times and sample prompts.
[06:17] Daniel Ortiz: on observability, can you operator-level traces for token time breakdown? like tokenization vs kernel vs egress?
[06:27] Priya Rao: the Console exposes per-token breakdowns with trace hooks, but sometimes we need a deeper trace. we can emit an annotated trace for the bench run. note: the agent may mislabel kernel time as "compute" in the exported CSV, we've seen that happen.
[06:45] Marcus Lee: excellent. any update on the quantization experiment you mentioned last week — did that affect perf here?
[06:53] Priya Rao: the quantized variant had lower compute per token but increased memory pressure during KV warmup which can exacerbate thrash if routing is unstable. it's unlikely the quantization alone caused the spike but it could have amplified it.
[07:07] Sara Patel: ok so action items recap?
[07:11] Jordan Kim: Jordan: send kernel/quant notes and rollback runbook by Wednesday. Priya: bench script and reproducible inputs by Friday. Sara: upload pcaps/traces by Thursday. Ethan: SOC2 packet and filtered KMS audit logs by Wednesday. Marcus: sign-off for canary rollback.
[07:31] Daniel Ortiz: sounds good. also small ask — can you add a short blurb on SAML/SSO behavior for service accounts? we want to confirm token lifetimes won't cause auth flaps during failovers.
[07:43] Ethan Cho: noted, will include SSO token lifetime references and recommended keepalive settings.
[07:50] Jordan Kim: ok great, thanks everyone. we'll target an hour-long bench run next week and reconvene with data. any last questions?
[07:59] Marcus Lee: nothing else, appreciate quick turnaround.
[08:03] Jordan Kim: thanks all, meeting adjourned.
